# Caching

## What this is

A hand-built, in-process read cache sitting in front of a deliberately slow "origin" store, so the mechanism is visible rather than hidden inside Redis. The origin is MongoDB reached through `repositories/products.js`, whose `findByIdSlow` (`src/repositories/products.js:16`) sleeps for `ORIGIN_DELAY_MS` and increments a module-level `originReads` counter on every call — that counter is the whole proof surface for "a cache hit does not touch the origin." The cache itself is a plain `Map` with per-entry expiry (`src/cache/store.js`) wrapped by a cache-aside loader that adds negative caching, TTL expiry, explicit invalidation on write, and — the centrepiece — single-flight coalescing of concurrent misses (`src/cache/productCache.js`). It answers "how do we serve the same read cheaply and correctly under load," not "how do we make one read fast" (that is an index problem, see [`../../../../sql-ledger/src/pagination/README.md`](../../../../sql-ledger/src/pagination/README.md)).

## How it works here

**Cache-aside, and where the layers sit.** `GET /api/products/:id` runs `controllers/products.js` → `services/products.js` `getProduct` → `cache.get(id)`. The service owns exactly one long-lived cache instance (`src/services/products.js:11`), wired with a loader that is the only thing that ever calls the slow origin: `loader: (id) => productsRepo.findByIdSlow(id)`. `cache.get` (`src/cache/productCache.js:17`) reads the store first; on a live entry it returns `{ value, source: 'cache' }` and the origin is never touched. On a miss it calls `load`, which awaits the loader, writes the result into the store, and returns `{ value, source: 'origin' }`. This is *cache-aside* (a.k.a. lazy loading): the application, not the store, is responsible for populating the cache, and a miss is a normal, expected event rather than an error. The `source` field is threaded all the way out to an `X-Cache` response header (`src/controllers/products.js:6`) so a caller can watch a cold read (`origin`) turn warm (`cache`) with nothing but `curl -i`.

**Only repositories touch Mongo; the cache is a separate store.** The repo-wide rule is that only `repositories/` import a Mongoose model and issue database calls, and `products.js` is the only file that imports `Product`. The in-process cache is not the database — it is the mechanism this guide is about — so it lives in `src/cache/` and is reached through the service, exactly as the token bucket in [`../../../../mern-tickets/server/src/throttle/README.md`](../../../../mern-tickets/server/src/throttle/README.md) is a mechanism the service calls rather than a repository. No service, cache, or repository module mentions `req` or `res`; the `X-Cache` header is set in the controller and nowhere else.

**TTL expiry.** Every entry carries an absolute `expiresAt = now + ttlMs` stamped at write time (`src/cache/store.js:13`), and `store.get` deletes and reports a miss the moment `expiresAt <= now` (`src/cache/store.js:6-9`). Write time means the moment the loaded value is actually stored, after the origin has resolved: the cache reads its injectable `clock` (`src/cache/productCache.js:7,12-13`) again at that point instead of reusing the timestamp captured when the miss began, because a miss-time stamp lets a slow origin silently eat the entry's life — a 900ms load against a 1000ms TTL would leave the entry 100ms to live. The clock defaults to `Date.now`, so the tests drive expiry deterministically by injecting `clock: () => t` and advancing `t` between reads (`test/ttlInvalidation.test.js` reads at `0`, `500`, `1500` against a `ttlMs` of `1000`) instead of sleeping. TTL is the cache's *safety valve*: even with no invalidation anywhere, a stale entry cannot outlive its TTL, so the worst-case staleness window is bounded by construction rather than by hoping every writer remembers to invalidate.

**Explicit invalidation on write.** TTL alone means a write is invisible to readers until the entry expires. `updateProduct` (`src/services/products.js:33`) closes that window: it writes through the repository and then calls `cache.invalidate(id)` (`src/cache/productCache.js:33`), deleting the entry so the very next read is a miss that reloads the new value. The `test/ttlInvalidation.test.js` "serves a stale value..." test makes the gap concrete — it reads a value, mutates the origin underneath the cache, reads again and *asserts the stale value is still served* (`source: 'cache'`), then invalidates and reads the fresh value. The stale read is not a bug the test tolerates; it is the behaviour the test pins, because a cache that could never go stale would not be a cache. TTL bounds staleness in time; invalidation removes it on the one event (a write) that we can actually observe. And here is the subtle race deleting the store entry alone does not close: a cache miss starts a load; while the origin is thinking, a write commits and calls `invalidate` — which finds nothing in the store to delete, because the value exists only as an unresolved promise; the load then resolves and writes the *pre-write* value with a full TTL, so the cache is stale for a whole TTL starting the instant after the write. That is why `invalidate` also consults the in-flight map (`src/cache/productCache.js:33-40`): it marks the matching flight as invalidated — the resolved load still returns its value to whoever is already awaiting it, but skips the store write (`src/cache/productCache.js:11-14`) — and drops the flight from the map, so a read arriving after the invalidate starts a fresh load instead of coalescing onto the doomed one. The "drops an in-flight load" test in `test/ttlInvalidation.test.js` pins exactly this interleaving with a gated loader.

**Negative caching.** A lookup for a key the origin does not have returns `null`, and `load` caches that absence as a *negative entry* (`src/cache/productCache.js:12`) — `store.set(key, null, negativeTtlMs, now, true)` — with its own, deliberately shorter `negativeTtlMs` (default 5s vs 30s). A second read for the same missing key returns `{ value: null, source: 'negative' }` without a second origin call. This is what stops a flood of requests for a non-existent id (a scanning bot, a broken client, a deleted product still linked somewhere) from turning every one of them into an origin round-trip. The TTL is shorter on purpose: a negative entry is a bet that the key will *stay* absent, and that bet should be re-checked sooner than a positive value, because "this was just created" is a common transition and "this just got deleted" is not one you want to cache for long.

**Single-flight (the centrepiece).** The dangerous case is a *cold* popular key: it is not in the cache, and N requests for it arrive within the same origin round-trip. Naive cache-aside has every one of them miss, every one of them call the origin, and every one of them write the same value back — the cache stampede (a.k.a. thundering herd, dog-piling). `cache.get` prevents this with an in-flight promise map (`src/cache/productCache.js:8,20-31`): the first caller to miss stores a record carrying its pending load promise in `inflight` *before* awaiting it, and every subsequent caller that arrives while that promise is unresolved finds it via `inflight.has(key)` and awaits the *same* promise, returning `{ ..., source: 'coalesced' }`. Exactly one origin call is made no matter how many callers pile on; the `finally` removes the record — and only its own record, since an `invalidate` may already have dropped it and a newer flight may have taken its place — so the *next* cold read after settlement starts a fresh flight. `test/stampede.test.js` fires 20 concurrent `get`s at one cold key against a 25ms origin and asserts `state.calls === 1`, one `'origin'` and nineteen `'coalesced'`; the companion test constructs the same cache with `coalesce: false` and asserts the naive path makes all 20 calls. The coalescing is correct only because JavaScript is single-threaded: the first caller runs synchronously up to its first `await` — long enough to populate `inflight` — before any other caller's turn on the event loop, so there is no check-then-act gap for a competitor to slip through. That last clause is the whole reason this is safe *in one process* and is exactly the property it loses across processes (see "What this toy skips").

**The stats endpoint.** `GET /api/cache/stats` returns `{ size, originReads }` (`src/controllers/cache.js:3`) and `POST /api/cache/reset` clears the store and zeroes the counter — the two are there so the "Try it" section below can show the origin-call count staying flat while reads are served, which is the entire value proposition made observable.

## The core concepts

- **Cache-aside vs write-through vs write-behind — who writes the cache, and when.** *Cache-aside* (this app) puts the application in charge: read checks the cache, populates on miss; write goes to the origin and then invalidates (or updates) the cache. *Write-through* routes writes *through* the cache, which synchronously writes to the origin before acknowledging — the cache is never stale but every write pays the origin latency and the cache fills with data that may never be read. *Write-behind* (write-back) acknowledges the write to the cache immediately and flushes to the origin asynchronously — fast writes, but now the cache holds durable state the origin has not seen yet, so a crash loses acknowledged writes and you have re-invented the durability problems of a database inside your cache. This app is cache-aside because reads dominate, staleness is tolerable within a TTL, and the origin remains the single source of truth — the cache holds nothing that isn't reconstructible from Mongo.
- **TTL is a bound on staleness; invalidation is its removal on a known event.** These are not alternatives, they are layers. TTL is the guarantee that holds *even when you forget to invalidate*: no entry is older than its TTL, full stop, which is why a system with only TTL is still correct-ish and a system with only invalidation is one missed hook away from serving a wrong value forever. Invalidation is the optimisation that removes staleness on the one event you can actually observe — a write through your own service. You want both: TTL as the floor, invalidation as the fast path. Note the failure mode invalidation cannot cover — a change to the origin that does *not* go through your service (a DBA's manual `UPDATE`, another service writing the same collection) is invisible to `cache.invalidate`, and only the TTL will ever catch it.
- **The stampede is a concurrency bug, not a capacity bug.** It is tempting to think a stampede is just "too much load," but the giveaway is that it happens on a *single* cold key: the extra origin calls are not extra work the system was asked to do, they are duplicate work caused by a check-then-act race between concurrent misses. Single-flight fixes it by making the second-through-Nth callers *wait for the first* instead of racing it — which is why it is the same shape of fix as an idempotency claim or a compare-and-swap: collapse concurrent attempts at the same thing down to one winner. Contrast the mechanism, though: [`../../../../mern-shop/server/src/idempotency/README.md`](../../../../mern-shop/server/src/idempotency/README.md) collapses concurrent *writes* to one using a database unique index as the arbiter — a cross-process, durable claim — whereas single-flight collapses concurrent *reads* using an in-memory promise map that is per-process and evaporates on restart. Both answer "many callers, one effect"; one is durable and distributed, the other is a local latency optimisation, and confusing the two is how you end up trusting an in-memory map to dedupe a payment.
- **Single-flight is not a lock, and that matters for what it can promise.** No caller is blocked from proceeding; the coalesced callers are *awaiting a value*, not *holding a resource*. If the single flight fails (the loader throws), every awaiter sees the same rejection — which is usually what you want (fail the batch together) but means one flaky origin call fails N requests instead of one; the "propagates a loader failure" test in `test/stampede.test.js` pins that fate-sharing, and that a failed load caches nothing. A distributed cache-stampede lock (see the real-world section) has the opposite bias: it serialises, can dogpile-protect across processes, and has to worry about the lock holder dying — which an in-process promise never does, because if the process dies there are no awaiters left to strand.
- **Negative caching trades a staleness risk for a load bound, and the TTL is the price.** Caching absence is caching a fact that is unusually likely to change (things get created), so the negative TTL is the knob that says how long you are willing to serve "not found" for something that now exists. Too long and a just-created resource 404s for users who ask early; too short and you have not actually bounded the load from a key that really is permanently absent. There is no free value here — this app picks 5s as a deliberately conservative default and says so.
- **HTTP caching is the same ideas one layer out, expressed in headers instead of a Map.** Everything above is *server-side* caching inside one service. HTTP caching pushes caching toward the client and the network using response headers, and it is worth seeing the correspondence: `Cache-Control: max-age=N` is a TTL, handed to the browser and any shared cache (CDN, reverse proxy) instead of kept in a local Map; `s-maxage` is a separate TTL for *shared* caches specifically; `Cache-Control: no-store` opts out entirely; `stale-while-revalidate` is the header form of the pattern this toy skips (serve stale, refresh in the background). Validation is the interesting part: a response carries an `ETag` (an opaque version token for that representation) or `Last-Modified`, and a client revalidating a possibly-stale entry sends `If-None-Match: "<etag>"` (or `If-Modified-Since`); if it still matches, the server returns **304 Not Modified** with an empty body, so the expensive part (the payload) is skipped even though a round-trip still happens. A CDN is just a shared HTTP cache living at the network edge, close to users, honouring these same headers — cache-aside implemented by Cloudflare/CloudFront/Fastly on your behalf, with your origin as the loader. **This is a genuinely different use of the word ETag from the one elsewhere in this repo.** In [`../../../../mern-tickets/server/src/concurrency/README.md`](../../../../mern-tickets/server/src/concurrency/README.md) the ETag is a *strong* validator used with `If-Match` on a *write* to prevent lost updates — a concurrency control that returns **412** on mismatch. Here the ETag is a (typically *weak*) validator used with `If-None-Match` on a *read* to save bandwidth — a cache optimisation that returns **304** on a match. Same header, opposite request header (`If-Match` vs `If-None-Match`), opposite success case (mismatch is the interesting one for concurrency; match is the interesting one for caching), different status code. Reading the two guides side by side is the fastest way to stop conflating them.
- **The cache key is a contract.** This app keys on the product id alone, which is correct only because `GET /api/products/:id` returns one representation for everyone. The moment a response varies by caller — role-based redaction (as the tickets app does), locale, currency, auth — the key has to include whatever it varies on, or you will serve one user's representation to another. HTTP formalises exactly this hazard with the `Vary` header. A cache key that is coarser than the thing it caches is a data-leak bug, not a performance bug.
- **What actually belongs in a cache.** Read-heavy, recomputation-expensive, staleness-tolerant, and reused across requests — all four. Data that is written as often as read gets little benefit and a lot of invalidation complexity; data that must be exactly current (a balance at checkout, see [`../../../../sql-ledger/src/ledger/README.md`](../../../../sql-ledger/src/ledger/README.md)) should not be cached behind a TTL at all; per-request data reused nowhere is better handled by a request-scoped memo (an N+1 dataloader) than a shared cache.

## Standard practice

- Make cache-aside the default and keep the origin the source of truth — the cache should hold nothing you cannot rebuild by re-reading the origin, so a cold cache is a slow system, never a wrong one.
- Set a TTL on every entry even when you also invalidate — the TTL is the backstop for the writes you did not make through your own service and the invalidations you forgot; a cache with no TTL and one missed invalidation is stale forever.
- Invalidate (or update) on write, and do it in the same service method that performs the write, so the two cannot drift apart — this app calls `cache.invalidate(id)` immediately after `productsRepo.update` in `updateProduct`.
- Coalesce concurrent misses on the same key (single-flight) for anything whose origin load is slow or popular — it is the cheapest protection against the stampede and, unlike raising the TTL, it does not trade staleness for load.
- Give negative entries their own, shorter TTL — absence changes more readily than presence, and reusing the positive TTL either over-serves 404s or under-protects the origin.
- Put the cache key's full variance in the key (role, locale, currency, auth), or you will serve one caller's representation to another — coarser-than-the-data keys are a correctness bug.
- Decide and document whether a coalesced/failed load fails the whole batch — single-flight ties N callers' fate together, which is usually right for a read but must be a deliberate choice.
- Measure hit rate and origin-call rate, not just latency — a cache with a 5% hit rate is mostly overhead, and you cannot tell without the counter this app exposes at `/api/cache/stats`.

## What this toy skips

- **No distributed cache, and single-flight is per-process.** The `Map` and the in-flight promise map live in one Node process. Run two instances behind a load balancer and you have two independent caches with two independent single-flight groups: a cold popular key can still stampede the origin with *one call per process*, not one call total. The in-process promise map cannot coordinate across processes at all — that coordination is exactly what a shared cache with a distributed lock (or a request-collapsing CDN) buys, and it is the single biggest thing this toy does not have. The contrast with [`../../../../mern-shop/server/src/idempotency/README.md`](../../../../mern-shop/server/src/idempotency/README.md) is the lesson: a unique index dedupes across every process because the arbiter is the shared database; a promise map dedupes only within the process that holds it.
- **No eviction policy — the cache only shrinks on expiry or invalidation.** There is no maximum size and no LRU/LFU/FIFO/ARC eviction. A workload that reads a very large number of distinct keys within a single TTL window grows the `Map` unboundedly until entries expire; a real cache is memory-bounded and evicts the coldest entries under pressure. This app relies entirely on TTL to reclaim space, which is fine for a small catalogue and wrong for a large or adversarial keyspace.
- **No cross-instance coherence.** An invalidation on one instance does not reach the others; each instance only invalidates its own copy. Sibling instances keep serving the old value until their own TTL expires. Real distributed caches solve this with a shared store (everyone reads the same Redis) or a pub/sub invalidation broadcast; neither exists here.
- **TTL is checked lazily, on read, never swept.** An entry that is never read again after it expires sits in the `Map` until something asks for its key. There is no background reaper, so "expired" and "freed" are not the same moment — memory is reclaimed on the next `get` for that key, or never.
- **No stale-while-revalidate, no probabilistic early expiration.** When an entry expires here, the next reader pays the full origin latency (a latency spike at every TTL boundary for a hot key). Stale-while-revalidate would serve the stale value instantly and refresh in the background; probabilistic early expiration (the XFetch approach) would have one reader refresh slightly *before* expiry so the herd never all miss at the same instant. This app implements neither — single-flight handles the *cold-key* herd, but a *hot-key TTL-boundary* herd (everyone misses the microsecond the TTL lapses) is only softened by single-flight, not eliminated.
- **No write-through or write-behind option.** Writes always go to the origin and invalidate; the cache is never written to directly.
- **No HTTP caching on the wire.** The app sets an `X-Cache` diagnostic header but does not emit `Cache-Control`, `ETag`, or honour `If-None-Match`/`304` — the HTTP-caching discussion above is prose, not implemented here. That layer is genuinely additive and would sit in a middleware in front of these routes.
- **The origin-call counter is process-global module state.** `originReads` is a module-level integer, which is exactly why the tests call `resetCacheStats()` between cases. It is a teaching probe, not a metric you would ship — real cache metrics are per-key-space, exported to Prometheus, and never reset by an HTTP endpoint (see [`../../../../mern-tickets/server/src/observability/README.md`](../../../../mern-tickets/server/src/observability/README.md)).

## In the real world (AWS / GCP)

The pieces map onto managed services layer by layer; what stays your code is the invalidation logic and the key design.

- **The in-process `Map` becomes a shared cache.** On AWS that is **ElastiCache** (Redis or Memcached) or **MemoryDB** (Redis-compatible but durable, with a multi-AZ transaction log — the difference matters when the "cache" is holding data you cannot afford to lose on failover). On GCP it is **Memorystore** (Redis or Memcached). The moment the cache is shared, invalidation becomes coherent across instances for free (everyone reads the same store) — the cross-instance incoherence in "What this toy skips" simply disappears, at the cost of a network hop per cache access and a new piece of infrastructure to run.
- **Single-flight moves, and mostly stops being your code.** Across processes you cannot coalesce with an in-memory promise, so the request-collapsing lives elsewhere: a distributed lock in Redis (`SET key value NX PX ttl` as the claim, the same conditional-write shape as the idempotency guide), or — far more commonly — the CDN does it for you. **CloudFront** and **Cloud CDN** both collapse concurrent cache misses for the same object into a single origin fetch (CloudFront calls it *origin shielding*/request collapsing; Fastly and Cloudflare do the same). If your reads are HTTP-cacheable, the cheapest stampede protection is to stop hand-rolling it and let the edge coalesce.
- **TTL and validation become response headers at the edge.** `Cache-Control: max-age`/`s-maxage`, `ETag` + `If-None-Match` → `304`, and `stale-while-revalidate` are honoured directly by CloudFront / Cloud CDN / API Gateway caching. This is the same cache-aside pattern with the CDN as the cache and your service as the loader — you configure it rather than write it.
- **DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)** is the special case worth naming: a write-through cache bolted directly onto DynamoDB, so reads hit the cache and writes go through it and stay coherent, with no invalidation code of your own. It is the managed form of the write-through option this toy skips, valid precisely because it is welded to one database's write path.
- **What stays your code no matter what you buy.** The key design (what varies, what `Vary`s), the decision of *what* is safe to cache and for how long, and the invalidation-on-write call in your service method. A managed cache gives you storage, eviction, coherence, and often request-collapsing; it does not know that *this* write should evict *that* key. That mapping is domain logic and it stays with you — which is the same conclusion the [`../../../../sql-jobs/src/queue/README.md`](../../../../sql-jobs/src/queue/README.md) and [`../../../../mern-tickets/server/src/throttle/README.md`](../../../../mern-tickets/server/src/throttle/README.md) real-world sections reach about their own mechanisms: the infrastructure absorbs the plumbing, the correctness decisions do not migrate.

## Try it

```bash
cd mern-cache/server
npm install
cp .env.example .env
npm run seed
npm run dev
```

Grab a product id and reset the counters, then read the same product twice and watch `X-Cache` go from `origin` to `cache` while `originReads` stays at 1:

```bash
id=$(curl -s http://localhost:5006/api/products | node -pe 'JSON.parse(require("fs").readFileSync(0,"utf8"))[0]._id')
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:5006/api/cache/reset >/dev/null

curl -s -o /dev/null -D - "http://localhost:5006/api/products/$id" | grep -i x-cache
curl -s -o /dev/null -D - "http://localhost:5006/api/products/$id" | grep -i x-cache
curl -s http://localhost:5006/api/cache/stats
```

```
X-Cache: origin
X-Cache: cache
{"size":1,"originReads":1}
```

Single-flight, made visible. Reset, then fire ten concurrent reads at one cold key and check the counter — with the 15ms origin delay they overlap, and only one reaches the origin:

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:5006/api/cache/reset >/dev/null
for i in $(seq 1 10); do curl -s -o /dev/null "http://localhost:5006/api/products/$id" & done; wait
curl -s http://localhost:5006/api/cache/stats
```

```
{"size":1,"originReads":1}
```

Ten simultaneous misses, one origin call. (Bump `ORIGIN_DELAY_MS` in `.env` if your machine is fast enough to resolve the first read before the others start — a larger window makes the coalescing unambiguous.)

Invalidation on write. Read once to warm the cache, update the price, read again and see the new value with `X-Cache: origin` because the write evicted the entry:

```bash
curl -s -o /dev/null -D - "http://localhost:5006/api/products/$id" | grep -i x-cache
curl -s -X PATCH "http://localhost:5006/api/products/$id" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"priceCents":111}'
curl -s -D - "http://localhost:5006/api/products/$id" | grep -iE 'x-cache|priceCents'
```

Negative caching. Ask for an id that does not exist twice; the second is a `negative` hit and the counter proves the origin was consulted once:

```bash
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:5006/api/cache/reset >/dev/null
curl -s -o /dev/null -D - http://localhost:5006/api/products/000000000000000000000000 | grep -i x-cache
curl -s -o /dev/null -D - http://localhost:5006/api/products/000000000000000000000000 | grep -i x-cache
curl -s http://localhost:5006/api/cache/stats
```

```
X-Cache: origin
X-Cache: negative
{"size":1,"originReads":1}
```

## Further reading

- [AWS Prescriptive Guidance — Caching best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/caching-best-practices/welcome.html) — cache-aside vs write-through vs write-behind laid out plainly, with the read/write ratio and staleness tolerance as the deciding variables, which is the framing this guide uses.
- [RFC 9111, HTTP Caching](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html) — the actual definition of `Cache-Control`, `max-age`/`s-maxage`, freshness, and validation; the authority for the HTTP-caching prose above.
- [RFC 9110 §13.1.2 & §15.4.5, `If-None-Match` and 304 Not Modified](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-if-none-match) — the read-side conditional request and its success code, the mirror of the write-side `If-Match`/412 pair the concurrency guide leans on.
- [RFC 5861, `stale-while-revalidate` and `stale-if-error`](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5861.html) — the header form of the serve-stale-then-refresh pattern this toy skips, and why the two directives are separate.
- [MDN — HTTP caching](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Caching) — the readable companion to RFC 9111, including a clear treatment of `Vary` and the cache-key hazard.
- [Redis — Client-side caching and the thundering herd](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/client-side-caching/) — request coalescing and cache invalidation from the store's own documentation, and the tracking-based invalidation model a shared cache adds on top.
- [Vattani, Chierichetti, Lowenstein — Optimal Probabilistic Cache Stampede Prevention (VLDB 2015)](https://www.vldb.org/pvldb/vol8/p886-vattani.pdf) — the XFetch algorithm behind probabilistic early expiration: refresh slightly early, with a probability that rises as expiry nears, so the herd never all misses at once.
- [Facebook/Meta — Scaling Memcache at Facebook (NSDI 2013)](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/conference/nsdi13/nsdi13-final170_update.pdf) — leases (their single-flight), the thundering-herd problem at real scale, and cross-region cache invalidation; the canonical war story for everything in "What this toy skips."
- [Amazon CloudFront — Origin request collapsing / origin shield](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudFront/latest/DeveloperGuide/origin-shield.html) — the CDN doing single-flight for you across the whole edge, which is where request coalescing lives once reads are HTTP-cacheable.

Elsewhere in this repo: [`../../../../mern-tickets/server/src/concurrency/README.md`](../../../../mern-tickets/server/src/concurrency/README.md) is the one to read alongside this — the *same* ETag header used for the opposite job (write-side lost-update prevention with `If-Match`/412, versus read-side revalidation with `If-None-Match`/304). [`../../../../mern-shop/server/src/idempotency/README.md`](../../../../mern-shop/server/src/idempotency/README.md) for the durable, cross-process version of "collapse concurrent attempts into one" that single-flight does only in-process. [`../../../../mern-tickets/server/src/throttle/README.md`](../../../../mern-tickets/server/src/throttle/README.md) and [`../../../../mern-shop/server/src/rateLimit/README.md`](../../../../mern-shop/server/src/rateLimit/README.md) for the lazy, compute-on-read pattern the TTL store shares with lazy token refill. [`../../../../mern-tickets/server/src/circuitBreaker/README.md`](../../../../mern-tickets/server/src/circuitBreaker/README.md) for the other in-process, per-instance mechanism whose state does not survive a restart and does not coordinate across processes — the same honest limitation this cache carries.
